title: Smoothed singular-value energies
subtitle: Quadratic behavior, Hilbert–Schmidt domains and gradients
adaptation: Mathematical companion outlining the definitions, argument, worked cases, and scope of the source lecture.

slides.title: Smooth a nuclear-type penalty
slides.lead: A smooth scalar cost can change the finite-energy operator ideal.
body: Subtracting tau from the square root normalizes the cost to vanish at zero. Its quadratic behavior for small singular values determines the domain of the infinite sum.

slides.title: Rationalization exposes the domain
slides.lead: The algebraic identity separates near-zero and large-s behavior.
body: Multiplying by the conjugate sum shows that the cost is quadratic for s much smaller than tau and approximately linear for s much larger than tau.

slides.title: Smooth and convex
slides.lead: The scalar penalty has a zero derivative at the origin.
body: Its first derivative is bounded by one, and its strictly positive second derivative makes it convex. Smoothing removes the sharp cusp of the absolute-value penalty.

slides.title: Uniform quadratic comparison on bounded spectra
slides.lead: Every singular value lies below the operator norm M.
body: Rationalization gives lower and upper multiples of s squared. The constants depend on tau and M but are positive and finite for each fixed tau>0.

slides.title: Finiteness means Hilbert–Schmidt
slides.lead: The infinite-dimensional domain follows by summing the bounds.
body: For a compact operator, the smoothed singular-value energy is finite exactly when its squared singular values are summable: the Hilbert–Schmidt class.

slides.title: A separating diagonal example
slides.lead: One operator belongs to S₂ but not S₁.
body: Let the diagonal singular values be 1/n. The squared series converges and the ordinary singular-value sum diverges, but the smoothed energy is finite for every fixed positive tau.

slides.title: The zero-smoothing limit can diverge
slides.lead: Pointwise scalar convergence does not control infinite sums automatically.
body: As tau decreases, the smoothed penalties grow monotonically to each singular value. For the 1/n example, the cost tends to infinity by monotone convergence.

slides.title: Why the cost is not a norm
slides.lead: The small-value behavior is quadratic, so homogeneity fails.
body: For small s, doubling s roughly quadruples its cost. A norm would double instead. It is better to call the construction a spectral energy.

slides.title: Finite-matrix gradient
slides.lead: The gradient does not divide by any singular value.
body: For a rectangular matrix, differentiate the trace of the shifted matrix square root. The positive tau gives a bounded inverse square root even at rank deficiency.

slides.title: A useful three-part checklist
slides.lead: A scalar penalty, its natural ideal, and its limiting topology are separate choices.
body: A smooth formula does not by itself guarantee a finite trace on every bounded operator. Check summability at small singular values before differentiating or passing to a smoothing limit.
slides.mathtex: T\in S_2\quad\text{is the finite-cost condition for }\tau>0
slides.takeaway: The small-singular-value asymptotics determine the ideal.
